lead: Ohm's law fixes the voltage across a resistor once its current is known. Kirchhoff's two laws do the bookkeeping for everything else: charge cannot pile up at a node, and energy per charge must return to its starting value after a closed loop. Together the three rules turn any circuit into a set of linear equations you can solve. Every practical check — the 220 Ω series resistor for an LED, the divider that feeds a 5 V regulator, the feeder currents in a Chennai street — ends in these laws.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1 for what R, L, C do, and Chapter 1.2 for the sources that push current round a loop.

blocks.text: A resistor is a two-terminal element. Ohm's law says the voltage across it is proportional to the current through it, and the constant of proportionality is the resistance. It holds for an ohmic element: a metal wire at fixed temperature, or a carbon film resistor well inside its power rating. A diode, a filament lamp or an LED is not ohmic, and the same formula does not describe it.
v = i R    i = v / R = v G
blocks.where: v is the voltage across the resistor in volts (V); i is the current through it in amperes (A); R is the resistance in ohms (Ω); G = 1/R is the conductance in siemens (S), so 1 S = 1 A/V.

blocks.text: Current enters the resistor at the terminal of higher potential and leaves at the lower one. Draw the arrow from the + terminal to the − terminal through the element; then v and i come out positive together. The resistor converts electrical energy into heat at the rate p = i²R watts, which is why every resistor carries a power rating.

A node is a point where two or more elements meet (Chapter 1.4). Kirchhoff's current law (KCL) says the algebraic sum of the currents at a node is zero. Charge does not accumulate at a point inside a conducting circuit: every coulomb that arrives must leave. That is conservation of charge, written at a node.

blocks.where: i is each branch current at the node, in amperes, written with + if it enters and − if it leaves — or the reverse, but the same choice for every term.

items: Mark a reference arrow on every branch that joins the node. Each arrow is that current's positive direction; a negative answer only means the real flow is opposite.
Choose one convention: entering positive and leaving negative, or leaving positive and entering negative.
Write every current with its sign and set the total to zero.
Solve, then redraw any arrow whose answer came out negative.

blocks.text: The same rule works for a whole region of a circuit: the sum of currents leaving any closed boundary is zero. That is how a supernode is handled in Unit 2.

Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL) says the algebraic sum of the voltages around any closed loop is zero. A charge that travels round a loop and returns to its starting point has the same potential energy per coulomb as when it started. Voltage is energy per unit charge, so the rises and the drops must cancel exactly.

blocks.where: v is each element voltage round the loop, in volts, written with + for a rise and − for a drop while you walk the loop in one chosen direction.

items: Choose a loop: a closed path that does not pass through the same node twice.
Choose a walking direction, clockwise or anticlockwise, and keep it for the whole loop.
Entering a terminal marked − and leaving at + is a rise: write +v.
Entering + and leaving at − is a drop: write −v.
Sum to zero. Equivalently, sum of rises = sum of drops.

blocks.text: KVL also holds along an open path if you add the voltage between the two ends. That reading gives the loop equations of mesh analysis in Unit 2.

sections.h3: Open circuit, short circuit, and AC

blocks.text: Ohm's law has two degenerate cases. An open circuit is a break: no current flows whatever voltage stands across the gap, so i = 0 and R = ∞. A short circuit is a zero-resistance link: the voltage across it is zero whatever current it carries, so v = 0 and R = 0. Swapping the two ruins a whole solution.

Both Kirchhoff laws are general. They hold at every instant with instantaneous values, so they describe AC as well as DC. In sinusoidal steady state you write them for phasors: ΣI = 0 at a node and ΣV = 0 round a loop, with complex I and V (Unit 3). Ohm's law becomes V = I Z, where Z is the impedance in ohms.
Counting equations: a connected network with n nodes and b branches gives n − 1 independent KCL equations and b − n + 1 independent KVL equations. Chapter 1.8 explains where those counts come from.

figure.caption: One sign assignment feeds both laws: KCL adds the currents at a node and KVL adds the voltages round a loop, and each pair of hands the same kind of equation to the solver.

spec.title: KCL and KVL

examples.question: (a) One branch carries 2 A into a node, and two other branches carry 0.8 A and 0.5 A out of it. A third leaving branch carries I3; find I3. (b) A 12 V source drives a loop current through elements with voltage drops of 3 V and 5 V, and through one more element with voltage Vx; find Vx. (c) A 12 Ω resistor carries 0.5 A; find the voltage across it.
steps: Take entering as positive and leaving as negative, and apply KCL at the node: 2 − 0.8 − 0.5 − I3 = 0.
I3 = 2 − 0.8 − 0.5 = 0.7 A. The sign is positive, so it leaves the node as drawn.
Walk the loop in the direction of the source. The 12 V source is a rise and the three element voltages are drops, so KVL gives 12 − 3 − 5 − Vx = 0.
Vx = 12 − 3 − 5 = 4 V, a drop in the chosen direction.
Ohm's law on the 12 Ω resistor: v = i R = 0.5 A × 12 Ω = 6 V.
Check: 2 − 0.8 − 0.5 − 0.7 = 0 for KCL; 12 − 3 − 5 − 4 = 0 for KVL; and 6 V across 12 Ω gives 6/12 = 0.5 A.
examples.answer: I3 = 0.7 A leaving the node, Vx = 4 V, and the 12 Ω resistor has 6 V across it.
examples.check:
i_in = 2.0
i_a = 0.8
i_b = 0.5
i3 = i_in - i_a - i_b
print(round(i3, 6))
vs = 12.0
d1 = 3.0
d2 = 5.0
vx = vs - d1 - d2
print(round(vx, 6))
r = 12.0
i = 0.5
print(round(r * i, 6))

traps: Mixing entering and leaving currents in the same sum: a leaving current added with a plus sign next to entering ones can never give zero. Fix the convention before writing the first term.
Adding a rise and a drop with the same sign. A 12 V source is +12 V walked one way and −12 V walked the other; the total is still zero, but every individual answer flips sign.
Using the source voltage in Ohm's law instead of the voltage across that resistor. Ohm's law wants v across the element, not the battery behind it.
Unit slip with conductance: a 4 Ω resistor has G = 0.25 S, not 0.25 Ω. Siemens is the reciprocal unit, and the exam often asks for G to catch this.
Confusing the two degenerate cases: an open circuit has i = 0 for any v (R = ∞), a short circuit has v = 0 for any i (R = 0).

quiz.q: State KCL and KVL in one line each.
quiz.a: KCL: the algebraic sum of the currents at a node is zero. KVL: the algebraic sum of the voltages around a closed loop is zero.

quiz.q: Define conductance, give its symbol and its unit.
quiz.a: Conductance G = 1/R, the reciprocal of resistance; unit siemens (S), where 1 S = 1 A/V.

quiz.q: Why does KCL follow from conservation of charge?
quiz.a: Charge cannot accumulate at a node in a conducting circuit, so the total charge per second entering equals the total leaving; written algebraically with signs, the sum is zero.

quiz.q: Two resistors are joined at a single node and nothing else touches it. Which law forces the same current through both, and why?
quiz.a: KCL at the shared node. Only two branches meet there, so current in through one equals current out through the other; the two elements are in series.

quiz.q: A 220 Ω resistor carries 15 mA. Find the voltage across it and the power it dissipates.
At a node, 3 A and 1.2 A enter and 2.5 A leaves. Find the remaining current and its direction.
quiz.a: Entering positive: 3 + 1.2 − 2.5 − I = 0, so I = 1.7 A, positive, hence leaving the node.

quiz.q: For the loop of part (b) of the worked example, a student writes 12 + 3 + 5 + Vx = 0 and gets Vx = −20 V. Where is the error, and what is the correct value?
quiz.a: The student gave the source rise and the element drops the same sign. With the source as a rise and the element voltages as drops the loop must read 12 − 3 − 5 − Vx = 0, giving Vx = 4 V in the drop direction.

quiz.q: An open circuit has i = 0 for any voltage. Does that break Ohm's law?
quiz.a: No. Ohm's law still reads i = v/R; as R → ∞ the current tends to zero for any finite v. The open circuit is a limiting case, not an exception.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every SPICE simulator builds its matrix from exactly these three rules: a KCL row for each node, a branch relation for each element, then one linear solve. Power-system load flow does the same thing at city scale, with complex phasors instead of resistors. Search for modified nodal analysis, phasor-domain KCL, and nodal power flow if you want to see the industrial version.
